title: Distinguishing quantum processes with bounded coherent memory
abstract: Distinguishing multi-time quantum processes is a fundamental task underlying the diagnosis, benchmarking, and learning of temporally correlated quantum dynamics. The standard benchmark for distinguishing two processes is the strategy-norm distance, which optimizes over arbitrary adaptive probing strategies but can require large coherent memory and time-dependent control. We introduce machines for autonomous distinction~($\mathsf{MAD}$s): probing strategies that apply the same quantum instrument at each time step, retain the full classical outcome record, and carry a coherent memory of dimension $d_A$. Optimizing over these strategies defines a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure, $d^{(N)}_{\mathsf{MAD}}(\mathbf{P}^N,\mathbf{Q}^N;d_A)$. We show that the resulting hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and complete at finite times. Specifically, any admissible $N$-step probing strategy can be compiled into a single $\mathsf{MAD}$ with an internal counter and sufficiently large coherent memory, so the hierarchy saturates the strategy-norm benchmark. For recurrent processes generated by repeated system--environment interactions, we derive a single-step description that separates the generation of new distinguishing information from the propagation and decay of information generated at earlier times. Numerical results in a repeated-interaction model show that increasing coherent memory systematically improves the $\mathsf{MAD}$ success probability and closes the gap to the strategy-norm distance while remaining substantially more tractable to evaluate. $\mathsf{MAD}$ distinguishability therefore provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about genuinely multi-time quantum processes with bounded coherent memory.
summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of distinguishing complex, multi-time quantum processes due to exponentially scaling computational requirements. It introduces 'Machines for Autonomous Distinction' (MADs), which restrict testing strategies based on a bounded coherent memory dimension ($d_A$). This results in a scalable distinguishability measure that provides an operational lower bound on the true optimal discrimination capability.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a computationally tractable measure for distinguishing between two multi-time quantum processes ($P_N$ vs $Q_N$) when the optimal strategy requires an exponentially large coherent memory.
main_result: The introduction of Machines for Autonomous Distinction (MADs) provides a scalable, memory-constrained distinguishability measure that is proven to saturate the full strategy-norm benchmark as the available coherent memory dimension increases.
method: The authors restrict the set of admissible probing strategies to those compatible with bounded coherent memory ($d_A$), leading to a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure $d^{(N)}_{\mathsf{MAD}}$.
model_or_system: The study analyzes multi-time quantum processes, modeled using process tensors or quantum combs ($	ext{P}_N$), which represent the input-output behavior over sequential time steps via CPTP maps.
key_observables: Memory-parametrized distinguishability measure ($d^{(N)}_{\mathsf{MAD}}$), strategy-norm distance ($d_{	ext{str}}$), and the success probability of discrimination ($p^*_{	ext{succ}}$).
important_parameters: Coherent memory dimension ($d_A$), number of time steps ($N$), and the process tensors ($\mathbf{P}^N, \mathbf{Q}^N$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that restricting the tester to bounded coherent memory ($d_A$) provides a useful operational lower bound on the true distinguishability, which can be shown to converge to the full benchmark for finite $N$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate multi-time process discrimination as an operational task involving sequential probing and memory storage; one figure shows the interaction between a quantum comb ($	ext{PN}$) and a multi-time tester ($\{	ext{T}^j_N\}_j$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of the full strategy-norm distance, then introduces MADs as a memory-constrained alternative. It develops theoretical results showing monotonicity and completeness, derives single-step descriptions for recurrent processes, and concludes with numerical evidence demonstrating scalability.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial bridge between theoretically optimal but computationally intractable measures (like the strategy norm) and practically measurable quantities by quantifying the role of finite quantum memory in process characterization.

An experimenter probes a process at several times, stores information in memory, and obtains an outcome record (x0, x1, x2). Equivalently, a tester, i.e. a multi-time quantum instrument, is inserted into the slots of a process comb to produce statistics used to decide whether the pro- cess was PN or QN.

Each use of the instrument can be realized by a unitary interaction with an auxiliary probe followed by a projective measurement on the probe, its nonselective action being CPTP. In the au- tonomous implementation shown here, the unitary acts on the system and quantum memory, while a classical counter spec- ifies which output register stores the outcome and, if desired, allows explicit time dependence to be encoded internally.
